description:
Welcome to Earth Detector! 🌍

We're tackling NASA Space Apps Challenge's Be an Earth System Trend Detective! by combining NASA Earth observation data, climate science, and AI/ML to uncover meaningful environmental trends and communicate discoveries through compelling visualizations.
summary:
EarthSignal is an interactive web app that reveals when long-term changes in Saharan dust become detectable above natural variability. Using NASA MERRA-2 aerosol data from 1980 to 2026, it maps the Time of Emergence of dust trends across North Africa, the tropical Atlantic and the Caribbean. Users can change the season, start year, detection threshold and significance filter, then explore maps, regional time series and any single grid point.
The project addresses the challenge by acting as a trend detective: it separates real long-term signals from year-to-year noise and shows how robust each conclusion is. Following dust along its transport path, we found that the decline over the Sahara source region emerged in 2019, while downstream over the Atlantic and Caribbean the trend is not yet significant.
This matters because a trend can be real long before it becomes detectable. EarthSignal helps students, educators and researchers see not only whether Earth is changing, but when that change can be trusted.
details:
What it does

Saharan dust travels thousands of kilometers across the Atlantic every year. But dust levels can change so much from one year to the next that it is hard to tell whether we are seeing a long-term shift or just another year of natural variability.

That was the question behind EarthSignal: How do we know when a change is finally strong enough to stand out from the noise?

We built EarthSignal to explore that question using NASA's MERRA-2 aerosol data. It is an interactive web app that looks at dust trends from North Africa across the Atlantic to the Caribbean and estimates their Time of Emergence (ToE), the point when a long-term signal becomes detectable above natural variability.

Instead of only showing where dust is increasing or decreasing, EarthSignal asks when we have enough evidence to detect that change.

How it works

The idea is fairly simple. First, we look for a long-term trend. Then we ask whether that trend is strong enough to stand out from the usual year-to-year fluctuations.

Behind the scenes, EarthSignal uses Sen's slope to measure trends, an autocorrelation-adjusted Mann-Kendall test to check statistical significance, and a False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction because we are testing thousands of grid cells at once.

Next, we compare the accumulated trend signal with natural variability. We call a signal detectable when it crosses a chosen signal-to-noise threshold and stays beyond that threshold through the end of the record. This gives us a retrospective estimate of its Time of Emergence.

We also wanted people to be able to question the results rather than just accept one map. Users can switch between different dust variables, seasons, and starting years, adjust the detection threshold, and turn the significance filter on or off. They can even choose a single grid point and see its time series and signal-to-noise curve.

For places where a change has not yet emerged, EarthSignal can show when it might become detectable if the historical trend continues. These are conditional extrapolations, not forecasts, and the app makes that distinction clear.

What we found

One of the most interesting things we found was that the dust signal does not become detectable everywhere at the same time.

Looking at annual dust AOD from 2003 to 2025, the decline over the Sahara source region emerged in 2019. Farther south, the Sahel has only recently emerged, around 2025. But over the Atlantic corridor and the Caribbean, the trends are still not statistically significant.

In other words, we can detect a decline near the source, but we cannot yet make the same claim farther downstream.

Another result surprised us: the starting year makes a huge difference. Using the full record from 1980, 41.4% of the study area shows an emerged annual dust signal. Starting in 2003, that number drops to just 5.5%.

That does not necessarily mean the physical trend became weaker. The two periods have different lengths, and the satellite observing system also changed around 2000. It showed us how much our conclusions can depend on the data window we choose.

Benefits and intended impact

We wanted EarthSignal to make a complicated scientific idea easier to explore, especially for people who do not work with climate data every day.

Dust matters beyond the Sahara. It affects air quality across the Atlantic and carries nutrients that can influence ocean and terrestrial ecosystems. Understanding long-term changes in dust is therefore relevant to environmental and climate research.

But we think the bigger lesson goes beyond dust.

Not detecting a trend does not mean nothing is changing. And finding a trend does not automatically tell us how confident we should be in it.

EarthSignal gives students, educators, and researchers a way to explore that difference using real NASA data. Rather than presenting one answer as final, it lets users see how the evidence changes when they adjust the assumptions.

Tools and technologies

We used Python throughout the project.

We accessed NASA MERRA-2 data using earthaccess and cloud OPeNDAP, then worked with xarray, NumPy, and SciPy to process the data and calculate trends, statistical significance, and Time of Emergence.

For the interactive app, we used Streamlit and Plotly. GitHub was used for version control, and we deployed the app through Streamlit Community Cloud.

No special hardware was needed.

What makes it creative

There are already plenty of tools that show climate trends. We wanted to ask a slightly different question: When does a trend become detectable, and how much does that answer depend on the way we analyze the data?

For example, changing the signal-to-noise threshold from 2 to 1 can move the estimated emergence year several years earlier. Turning off the significance filter can make much more of the map appear to have emerged.

Instead of hiding those differences, we made them part of the app.

We think that is what makes EarthSignal different. It is not just a map of dust trends. It is a way to explore the evidence behind a scientific conclusion and understand why that conclusion might change.

Factors we considered

One challenge was that MERRA-2 is a reanalysis dataset, not a direct record of independent satellite measurements. Its observing system changed around 2000, so trends calculated from 1980 may partly reflect changes in the observations being assimilated.

That is why we included both 1980 and 2003 as starting years.

We also wanted to avoid calling something a real detection just because a statistical test happened to return a small p-value. We accounted for autocorrelation and applied FDR correction to reduce the risk of false discoveries when testing thousands of grid cells.

Another important distinction is that our Time of Emergence estimates are retrospective. If the app says a signal emerged in 2019, that means it stayed detectable through the end of the available record. It does not mean someone could necessarily have confirmed the change in real time in 2019.

The same goes for projected emergence years. They depend on the historical trend continuing, and they become especially uncertain when that trend is not statistically significant.

We tried to make these limitations visible rather than bury them in technical documentation. The app includes explanations of the methods and assumptions so users can understand not just what the results show, but also what they do not tell us.

A trend can be real long before it becomes detectable. That is the idea we wanted EarthSignal to communicate.
